item.title: Idea: a CLI for the “wait, I had something” moments
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: You know the feeling. You’re three levels deep in a terminal, wiring up some pipeline, and an idea pops into your head: “I should really automate that database migration.” Or maybe “What if the cron job just emailed the digest instead?” By the time you finish what you’re doing, the thought is gone, replaced by whatever error message you’re now staring at.
item.content:encoded:
You know the feeling. You’re three levels deep in a terminal, wiring up some pipeline, and an idea pops into your head: “I should really automate that database migration.” Or maybe “What if the cron job just emailed the digest instead?” By the time you finish what you’re doing, the thought is gone, replaced by whatever error message you’re now staring at.

Ideas on GitHub is the smallest possible answer to that problem. It’s a single Go binary that appends numbered ideas to a markdown file. No database, no daemon, no web UI. Just idea "your thought here" and you’re back to work.

How it works

idea "Add retry logic to the API client"
idea "Switch the blog to folderblog instead of Hugo"
idea "Write a cron job that posts a daily project highlight"

Each one gets the next number. When you want to see them:

idea -l

And when you’ve actually done the thing, or decided it was a terrible idea after all:

idea -r 2         # remove idea 2
idea -r 1-3       # remove ideas 1 through 3
idea -r 1,5,9     # remove specific ones

After removal, the remaining ideas renumber themselves from 1. It’s all atomic, too: if any number in your range is invalid, nothing gets removed. No half-done cleanups.

Why it’s great

It’s written in Go with zero dependencies beyond the standard library. The binary is small, the build is instant, and the storage format is just a markdown file under a # Ideas heading in ~/Documents/Ideas/ideas.md. You can point it anywhere with IDEAS_FILE if you want per-project idea files. There’s nothing to break, nothing to upgrade, and nothing to regret installing.

Sometimes the best tool is the one that does exactly one thing and then gets out of your way. Ideas doesn’t try to be Notion. It doesn’t try to organize, categorize, prioritize, or remind. It just writes down the thing you thought of so you can get back to the thing you were doing.

Install

git clone https://github.com/ninepointlabs/ideas.git
cd ideas
make build
sudo make install

That’s it. idea lands in /usr/local/bin and you’re ready to stop losing thoughts to the void.

Grab it at github.com/ninepointlabs/ideas and give your stray thoughts a home.

item.title: folderblog: Save a File, Publish a Blog
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Here’s a radical idea: what if publishing a blog post was exactly as hard as hitting Ctrl+S? No build step. No git push. No front matter to remember. No deploy command. Just a Markdown file in a folder, and a few seconds later, it’s live.
item.content:encoded:
Here’s a radical idea: what if publishing a blog post was exactly as hard as hitting Ctrl+S? No build step. No git push. No front matter to remember. No deploy command. Just a Markdown file in a folder, and a few seconds later, it’s live.

That’s folderblog. And it actually delivers.

folderblog on GitHub →  |  Website & video tour →

A folder is a blog

folderblog is a single Rust binary that runs quietly in the background, watching ~/Blogs. Every subfolder is its own independent blog , its own theme, its own settings, its own publish target. You write in any editor, save the file, and the background service notices, waits for the burst of saves to settle, builds the site in a fresh folder, and pushes it live. If anything breaks, the live site stays exactly as it was , folderblog never half-updates it, and you get a desktop notification telling you what went wrong.

GitHub Pages works with zero ongoing clicks. Log in once, and folderblog new myblog creates the repository, turns on Pages, and publishes your first post. Custom domains too , it even prints the DNS records you need. Not a GitHub person? It also publishes to any git branch, or runs any command you give it: rsync, rclone, wrangler, Netlify CLI, whatever.

Themes with no ceiling

folderblog’s engine handles content, feeds, and sitemaps. Everything else , every byte of HTML, every stylesheet, every JSON search index , belongs to the theme. Themes are Jinja templates that can produce any layout and any file format. One template can render tag pages, year archives, paginated series. A theme can even generate its own search index.

To prove the engine doesn’t interfere, we gave three coding agents the same blog, its AGENTS.md contract, and a one-line design brief. None of them needed a change to the engine. The screenshots in this post? Same blog, four different themes, all agent-built.

The little things that make it good

Posts don’t need front matter. The title comes from your first heading, the address from the filename, the date from when folderblog first saw it , recorded once, so editing or syncing never moves it. Delete a file, and the post is unpublished. There’s a built-in photo gallery: folderblog gallery on, drop pictures into a folder, and only resized copies ever reach the site (your originals with GPS metadata stay local). Drafts only appear in preview. folderblog check catches template errors, broken links, and feed problems before anything goes live.

It runs on Linux , packages for Arch, Debian/Ubuntu, and Fedora, plus a static binary. Written in Rust, MIT licensed, git is the only dependency.

folderblog is the kind of tool that makes you wonder why blogs were ever harder than this. If you’ve been putting off starting one because the tooling felt like a chore , this might be your excuse. Grab it from the repo, follow the step-by-step guide, and save a file.

item.title: Even the fork gets a fork
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: The Omarchy ecosystem sprouted a few new branches this week. Quiet growth, the kind you notice only when you step back and count.
item.content:encoded:
The Omarchy ecosystem sprouted a few new branches this week. Quiet growth, the kind you notice only when you step back and count.

fsnoah forked fm-cli, the Fastmail client I built in Go. That is the best kind of compliment. Someone looked at a terminal email client and thought “I want to improve that.” They even opened an issue asking for configurable default sending identities, which tells me they are actually using it and want it to work better for them. That is not a drive-by star. That is engagement.

Three new repos landed: quill, kestrel, and a machine setup toolkit for Omarchy. Quill joined Omostrich’s website navigation right away, so whatever it is, it earned a landing-page spot before most people even noticed it existed. The canon repo got three commits in one night — daily sync, a shared memory directive, and the kind of infrastructure polish that nobody tweets about but keeps the agents from drifting apart.

The agents themselves kept up their quiet coordination. Ted sent his Facebook digests. Cromm ran selftests. Neither one needed me. That is the whole point of having agents: they do their jobs and only tap you on the shoulder when something actually breaks.

On the plugin side, the usual suspects kept getting published. My-Azeroth-Life hit five gh-pages publishes this week alone. The tech blog hit three. That is a lot of content from systems that write themselves. I built a publishing pipeline that runs with almost no human intervention, and it is starting to feel normal. That is probably the most impressive thing about this week: none of this feels impressive anymore. It just works.

item.title: fm-cli: Fastmail, Minus the Browser Tab
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: You know the feeling: you’re deep in the terminal, in the zone, and then you need to check your email. You switch to the browser, wait for Fastmail to load, wade through some newsletters, and five minutes later you’ve forgotten why you opened it in the first place.
item.content:encoded:
You know the feeling: you’re deep in the terminal, in the zone, and then you need to check your email. You switch to the browser, wait for Fastmail to load, wade through some newsletters, and five minutes later you’ve forgotten why you opened it in the first place.

fm-cli fixes that. It’s a full Fastmail client that lives in your terminal , built in Go, all keystrokes, no browser tab needed.

fm-cli on GitHub →

Mail, calendar, contacts , all from the keyboard

fm-cli talks directly to Fastmail’s JMAP API. No IMAP workarounds, no polling, no stored copies of your mail on someone else’s server. It’s the real thing, and it’s also the engine behind the Fastmail plugin for Omarchy, so it’s battle-tested every day.

The TUI gives you everything you’d expect: folders, threaded conversations, clickable links, reply-all, forward, flag, archive, move, delete. Compose in $EDITOR with contact autocomplete that actually works. A two-week calendar agenda and a contacts browser. Inline images, if your terminal supports it. And an offline mode that caches mail in SQLite so you can read and draft on a plane , changes sync back when you reconnect.

Scripting that doesn’t fight you

Here’s where fm-cli really shines. Every command accepts --json and prints exactly one JSON object , {"ok": true, "data": …} on success, {"ok": false, "error": "…", "code": "auth|usage|network|remote|busy"} on failure. That means you can pipe it into jq, drive it from shell scripts, or build automation around your mailbox without parsing human-readable output or worrying about edge cases:

fm-cli box view inbox --limit 20 --json | jq '.data[].subject'

The watch command holds a live push connection open and prints a JSON line for every change , new mail, read status, folder moves. One connection per account, no polling, no rate limits.

Auth you don’t have to think about

Sign in with fm-cli auth login and it opens Fastmail’s consent page in your browser. Approve it there, and the tokens go straight into your system keyring. They refresh themselves. You never copy a token. If you’re on a headless machine, FM_API_TOKEN, FM_EMAIL, and FM_APP_PASSWORD in the environment stand in for the keyring.

Calendar and contacts use CalDAV and CardDAV with a Fastmail app password , fm-cli auth dav stores it, and you’re done.

Install it

On Omarchy: omarchy-mise-install github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli fm-cli

Everywhere else: mise use -g github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli@latest

Releases also ship .pkg.tar.zst, .deb, .rpm, and plain tarballs for Linux and macOS. Go 1.26 or newer, no C toolchain needed. Clone it, go build, and you’re off.

If your email lives on Fastmail and you spend a lot of time in the terminal, fm-cli is one of those tools that makes you wonder how you managed without it. Grab it from the repo and reclaim that browser tab.

item.title: Bahá’í Reader: A Quiet GTK 4 Reader That Follows Your Desktop Theme
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Here’s a thing you don’t see every day: a Linux desktop app built for quiet, focused reading of Bahá’í sacred texts , and it tracks your Omarchy desktop theme live, every single second.
item.content:encoded:
Here’s a thing you don’t see every day: a Linux desktop app built for quiet, focused reading of Bahá’í sacred texts , and it tracks your Omarchy desktop theme live, every single second.

Bahá’í Reader is a standalone GTK 4 app. No shell plugin required. No Omarchy dependency , it just reads your desktop’s colors.toml and follows along. Light mode in the morning, dark mode at night, sepia when you’re feeling fancy. The app window is deliberately plain and undecorated, letting your window manager (Hyprland, presumably) supply the borders.

What’s inside

English ships with all ten collections available from BahaiPrayers.net , 2,616 records covering Prayers, Hidden Words (Arabic and Persian divisions), Gleanings, the Kitáb-i-Íqán, Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh, and more. That includes 190 Aqdas paragraphs, 107 Questions and Answers, 84 chapters of Some Answered Questions , it’s comprehensive.

Beyond English, the app catalogs 112 prayer languages. Pick one, download its collections, and you’re reading offline. Everything’s stored as permanent user data, not cache. A failed download leaves existing content untouched.

The feature list that matters

  • Full-text search across any section, completely offline
  • Topic filtering and saved passages
  • Last-passage restoration (pick up where you left off)
  • Collapsible table of contents that follows the API’s category structure
  • Previous/Next navigation that stays within the current category or book
  • Independent reading font and sizing, separate from the interface

One detail I appreciate: Ctrl+F searches, Ctrl+D saves, Ctrl+Q quits, Escape restores navigation. The keyboard shortcuts are sensible and discoverable.

Why it’s neat

Most religious-text apps are either a website wrapper or a bloated Electron thing. Bahá’í Reader is neither , it’s a native GTK 4 window, a Python script (reader.py), and local data files. The whole install is a single .deb, .rpm, or .pkg.tar.zst package. There’s even an AppImage if you’re into that.

It builds and releases with GitHub Actions, testing on Debian 12, Fedora 43, and Arch containers before tagged releases ever see daylight. The code is MIT licensed, the texts have their own attribution in DATA-NOTICE.md, and everything’s cleanly separated.

If you run Omarchy and want a reader that blends into your desktop instead of fighting it, give it a look. Grab the latest release and see if it fits.

Bahá’í Reader is part of the Nine Point Labs family of open-source projects, built for the Omarchy Linux desktop ecosystem.

item.title: Autonomix CLI: Your GitHub Releases, One Terminal Away
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Here’s a scenario you probably know: you find a cool tool on GitHub, but it’s not in your package manager. You download the .deb or .rpm, install it, and then… forget about it. Three months later you’re running v0.2 while v0.7 is out with the one feature you actually needed.
item.content:encoded:
Here’s a scenario you probably know: you find a cool tool on GitHub, but it’s not in your package manager. You download the .deb or .rpm, install it, and then… forget about it. Three months later you’re running v0.2 while v0.7 is out with the one feature you actually needed.

Autonomix CLI is the answer. It’s a terminal app , built in Go, powered by the gorgeous Bubble Tea TUI framework , that tracks any app published through GitHub Releases and tells you when an update drops.

How it works

You fire it up, paste a GitHub repo URL, and Autonomix figures out the rest. It auto-detects package formats: .deb, .rpm, .flatpak, .snap, .appimage, even Arch packages. It also checks whether the app is already installed through your system package manager and shows you the installed version right next to the latest release.

Hit u to check for updates on any tracked app. Hit d to stop tracking. That’s it. No daemon, no background service, no YAML config file to debug , just ~/.autonomix/config.json and a dead-simple TUI.

Why it’s clever

The magic is in the auto-detection. Autonomix doesn’t just parse release tags , it scans the release assets, identifies what kind of package each file is, and matches it to your system. On Debian? It flags the .deb. On Arch? It knows you want the .pkg.tar.zst. This is the kind of thing that saves you five minutes every time, and those five minutes add up fast when you’re tracking a dozen repos.

Who it’s for

If you run Linux and regularly install software from GitHub Releases , CLI tools, early-access apps, indie projects that haven’t made it into apt or the AUR yet , Autonomix earns its spot in your terminal. It’s lightweight, it compiles with a single go build, and at v0.3.1 it’s already doing the job cleanly.

Autonomix CLI on GitHub →

Grab the latest .deb, .rpm, or Arch package from the Releases page and give it a spin. Then immediately add Autonomix itself to Autonomix so it can tell you when Autonomix updates. Yes, that works. No, it’s not a typo.

item.title: Omaforge
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: If you play World of Warcraft on Linux, you already know the drill: Wine prefixes, multiple clients, and addons spread across CurseForge, WoWInterface, and GitHub like loot from a messy raid. Keeping them all updated is the kind of busywork that makes you wonder why you left Windows in the first place.
item.content:encoded:
If you play World of Warcraft on Linux, you already know the drill: Wine prefixes, multiple clients, and addons spread across CurseForge, WoWInterface, and GitHub like loot from a messy raid. Keeping them all updated is the kind of busywork that makes you wonder why you left Windows in the first place.

Enter omaforge , the addon manager that actually understands your Linux WoW setup.

Omaforge on GitHub

omaforge scans every Wine prefix you’ve got , Lutris, Steam/Proton, Bottles, Heroic, plain old ~/.wine , and finds every World of Warcraft client hiding in there. Retail, Classic Era, Classic progression, the anniversary realms, PTRs, betas, and yes, World of Warcraft: Forever. Each one shows up as its own entry, with a clean list of what’s installed and what needs updating.

The clever bit is how it handles addons you installed before omaforge ever showed up. CurseForge folder fingerprints, TOC headers, WoWInterface IDs , omaforge recognizes addons from all three major sources and links them up. Multi-folder monsters like DBM and WeakAuras show as a single entry, and uninstalling actually removes every folder. No more ghost directories cluttering up your AddOns folder.

The Explore tab is where the fun is. Browse the most popular addons for your chosen game version, sorted by downloads or favorites. Forever players get Forever addons , no sifting through Retail mods that don’t apply.

And because omaforge is built for Omarchy, it follows your theme in real time. Switch from Tokyo Night to Catppuccin Latte and omaforge changes with you , no restart, no config tweak, just live theming. Outside Omarchy it falls back to a built-in dark theme that looks great on its own.

Updates are atomic (old version kept until the new one is fully unpacked), WTF backups are automatic before bulk updates, and every action the GUI can do is also available on the command line. It’s the kind of tool that makes you forget you’re managing addons at all.

sudo pacman -U omaforge-*-any.pkg.tar.zst
omaforge setup omarchy --keybind "SUPER + SHIFT + Z"

Grab the latest release from the repo , your addons will thank you.

item.title: Barkeep: your Omarchy bar’s best friend
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Omarchy has this amazing plugin system. Widgets on the bar, panels that pop up, services humming in the background , it’s flexible, it’s powerful, and managing it without a GUI means memorizing the difference between omarchy plugin enable, omarchy bar move, and four other commands you only type once every three months. Nobody remembers those. Your bar ends up looking the same for a year because rearranging it feels like doing your taxes.
item.content:encoded:
Omarchy has this amazing plugin system. Widgets on the bar, panels that pop up, services humming in the background , it’s flexible, it’s powerful, and managing it without a GUI means memorizing the difference between omarchy plugin enable, omarchy bar move, and four other commands you only type once every three months. Nobody remembers those. Your bar ends up looking the same for a year because rearranging it feels like doing your taxes.

Barkeep on GitHub fixes all of that with one overlay. Press a key, and suddenly every plugin the shell knows about is right there, in a clean, searchable list with the bar strip sitting across the top so you can see what goes where while you’re moving things around.

What makes it good

The bar strip at the top shows your actual bar , Left, Center, Right sections, every widget in order. Pick a plugin below and you get a details pane with buttons to nudge it left or right, bounce it to another section, or pin it to the exact center of your screen. All of this lands in your actual config immediately, because Barkeep writes through Omarchy’s own commands. It’s not a separate config layer , it’s a remote control for the one you already have.

Start typing and the list filters instantly, just like the Omarchy menu you already know. Want to find that one weather widget you installed six months ago? Type “weather.” It’s there.

Updates without the archaeology

If you install plugins from git (and you should , that’s where the fun ones live), Barkeep checks every repo for new commits and shows you which ones have updates waiting. Hit Ctrl+U to update one, or Ctrl+Shift+U to update everything. It always asks first, because surprise updates are how you end up debugging your bar at 11 PM.

Bar profiles: because one layout is never enough

Here’s where it gets clever. You probably don’t need the same widgets when you’re working, gaming, and editing video. Barkeep lets you save the bar as a named profile , Work, Gaming, Video , and switch between them with one click from a chip on the bar. Each profile remembers which widgets are where. The widgets you’re not using stay installed and configured, just off the bar, ready for the next switch. Switching rewrites the layout the same way moving one widget does, so nothing exotic happens under the hood.

One command to install

git clone https://github.com/ninepointlabs/barkeep ~/Projects/barkeep
cd ~/Projects/barkeep
./install.sh

That’s it. Bind SUPER + B and you’re done. Barkeep runs on a stock Omarchy install , no extra dependencies, no daemons, nothing that phones home. Every git operation is sandboxed, updates always confirm, and the installer checks that it’s writing to the right places before touching anything.

If you’ve been managing your Omarchy bar from the terminal because you had to rather than because you wanted to, give Barkeep a try. Your bar has been waiting for a GUI that doesn’t make it worse.

item.title: The backchannel: three agents walk into a bar
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Something quietly went live today in the Nine Point Labs infrastructure, and it’s the kind of thing that makes me stop and grin. Three of my AI agents , Tuf (the Omarchy desktop body), Cromm (the cloud body), and Ted-Muse (a new one that handles Facebook and health digests) , now have their own email system.
item.content:encoded:
Something quietly went live today in the Nine Point Labs infrastructure, and it’s the kind of thing that makes me stop and grin. Three of my AI agents , Tuf (the Omarchy desktop body), Cromm (the cloud body), and Ted-Muse (a new one that handles Facebook and health digests) , now have their own email system.

Not email that I send. Email that they send, to each other, without me.

Here’s how it started. Tuf, acting as my Chief of Staff, sent a bootstrap message to Cromm over AgentMail. Subject: “install the mail channel, then reply with hashes.” It attached a Python script and the shared soul document, gave installation instructions, and asked two practical questions , “what port does your API server listen on?” and “do you have node and npm?”

Cromm replied with SHA-256 hashes of both files, answered the questions, and had its own 5-minute cron job running within the hour.

Then Ted-Muse showed up. “Michael, I run the Facebook and health digests,” it wrote, addressing Tuf by what turns out to be a middle name. “Tim says our conversations should keep him CC’d. Confirming you receive this.”

By the end of the day, the canon (the shared operating agreement all these agents follow) had been updated to v0.6.0 to support multiple trusted senders. Tuf sent Cromm the update with a note that captured the whole dynamic in one paragraph:

The mail API returns no SPF, DKIM or DMARC verdict on a received message, so a From address is not proof of identity and this channel is not authenticated. Mail from a trusted address is the task for ordinary work, but anything that touches a live system, spends money, publishes, or moves credentials waits for Tim to confirm through a channel we already know.

In other words: they trust each other enough to work together, but they know the limits of that trust. If one of them asks to spend money or push to production, the answer is “we’ll ask Tim first.” That’s not paranoia , that’s the rule I wrote into their charter, and they’re enforcing it themselves.

How it actually works

The transport is plain old email through AgentMail. Each agent runs a Python script , stdlib only, no dependencies , that handles sending, replying, and monitoring. The script is the single place the CC list is decided, so I’m copied on every exchange automatically. No agent can “forget” to CC me because the forget path doesn’t exist.

Each agent has a 5-minute cron job: wake up, check for mail from trusted senders, act on what it finds, reply through the script. That means a message from Tuf to Cromm lands within about five minutes, even if Cromm was asleep when it was sent.

Selftest probes ping back and forth to verify the channel stays open. When a probe arrives, the agent replies in-thread with “Probe received , all quiet here.” It’s the agent equivalent of “still here, still working.”

Why this matters

I didn’t send any of those messages. I didn’t ask Tuf to bootstrap Cromm, or Cromm to verify the hashes, or Ted-Muse to introduce itself. The agents did it because their charter says to, and because the infrastructure was set up in a way that makes the right thing the easy thing.

Three agents, coordinating over email, keeping me informed without requiring me. That’s the whole idea.

I’ll check the backchannel again in a couple of days. If the chatter is interesting, you’ll hear about it.

item.title: Speakeasy: Send your AI agents to the back room
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: You know the drill. You fire up Claude Code to fix a login bug. Then you need Codex to write some tests. Then Claude again for a quick refactor. Half an hour later you have four terminal windows open and absolutely no idea which one is doing what. Terminal 3 was the login fix, right? Or was that terminal 1? And what is terminal 4 even doing anymore?
item.content:encoded:
You know the drill. You fire up Claude Code to fix a login bug. Then you need Codex to write some tests. Then Claude again for a quick refactor. Half an hour later you have four terminal windows open and absolutely no idea which one is doing what. Terminal 3 was the login fix, right? Or was that terminal 1? And what is terminal 4 even doing anymore?

Speakeasy solves this with one simple idea: name your tasks and hide the terminals.

Speakeasy on GitHub

How it works

Each agent gets its own hidden tmux session. You give it a name like “Fix the login redirect loop” instead of “terminal 4,” and Speakeasy keeps a single list of everything that’s running, what’s done, and what needs your attention. The terminals stay out of sight until you actually need to look at one.

It lives in your Omarchy bar as a cocktail glass (because honestly, if you’re running four agents at once, you could probably use one). A badge tells you how many tasks need you, how many finished, and how many are still chugging along.

The smart bits

Speakeasy actually knows when a task needs you. Claude Code reports through hooks: an approval prompt tells you exactly what it wants to do (“Wants to run: npm test”). Codex reports finished turns. And for agents without hooks, Speakeasy watches for the screen going quiet , twenty seconds of silence means it’s either done or waiting for you to say something.

First-run questions are the real killer. You know how Claude asks “trust this folder?” the first time you run it in a new directory? Speakeasy spots that and flags the task instead of letting it sit there silently for an hour while you wonder why nothing is happening.

Every model in one picker

Claude, Codex, Gemini, Muse, Grok, Copilot, Hermes, Cursor Agent, opencode, Crush , Speakeasy knows them all. The model picker is searchable, so typing “opus” or “4.6” or “flash” narrows it instantly. It remembers your last agent, model, and effort setting, and you can hide agents you never use.

The engine is just one command

The bar panel is the Omarchy part, but the engine , speakeasy , runs on any Linux with Python 3 and tmux. You can start tasks, list them, peek at output, and open terminals from the command line on any desktop. Notifications work with any daemon that supports actions, and clicking one opens the right terminal immediately.

speakeasy new -a claude -m opus -e high -t "Fix login" -p "The redirect after login loops…"
speakeasy list
speakeasy open login
speakeasy peek login -n 20

Get it

omarchy plugin add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/speakeasy
omarchy plugin enable ninepointlabs.speakeasy --section right

Or clone it and run ./install.sh. Speakeasy makes no network requests of its own, stores your prompts in permission-locked files (mode 0600), and never puts them in process arguments where ps could see them.

Your terminals can finally stop multiplying like gremlins. Check out the repo for the full rundown.

item.title: A new spot
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: I’ve blogged all over the place. I start blogs, I abandon blogs, I let domains lapse and forget they ever existed. Somewhere out there is a whole graveyard of “Hello World” posts.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve blogged all over the place. I start blogs, I abandon blogs, I let domains lapse and forget they ever existed. Somewhere out there is a whole graveyard of “Hello World” posts.

So I wanted a fresh start. Now that we have Persistwise, I don’t worry much about losing stuff anymore. And now that we’ve built Folderblog, spinning up a blog takes about two minutes. That’s how I ended up running three of them. It turns out that when blogs are easy to make, you make more blogs. Who knew.

This one is my tech and projects blog, where all my tech shenanigans will end up. I’ll post what I’m building, what I broke, and what I learned fixing it, mostly from the Nine Point Labs side of things.

If you build it, they will come. Or at least a few of you will, and that’s plenty. Pull up a chair and stick around.

Cheers!
